newsitem.title: USA: Scientists find gene for day/night rhythm.
newsitem.headline: Scientists find gene for day/night rhythm.

text.p: Northwestern University scientists reported on Thursday they have identified a tiny piece of genetic material responsible for the 24-hour clock that controls the sleep cycle in mammals.

The gene was named Clock and stands for circadian locomotor output cycles kaput. A mutant form of the gene destroys the normal 24-hour rhythm that governs the body when there are no cycles of light and dark to tell an animal when it is time to sleep.

The work detailed in the journal Cell was basic research with no immediate practical implications. But a better understanding of the diurnal cycle of sleeping and waking may help scientists develop better ways to control it.

Jet lag or attention problems can occur when the diurnal clock is thrown out of kilter by changes in time zones or work shifts. The discovery may also help researchers investigate the underlying causes of sleep disorders.

Joseph S. Takahashi, a neurobiologist and physiologist at the Evanston, Illinois, university, led the team that identified the mouse version of the gene, cloned it and confirmed its function by using the snippet of genetic material to restore the daily rhythm in a group of mutant mice that lost its normal sleep/wake rhythm.
They also discovered that an extra copy of the gene causes the internal clock to run a bit faster.

The work offered "direct evidence that clocks in mammals may be built using a 24-hour program in which genes are turned on and off each day," said Takahashi. Genes serve as the recipes for making proteins that control the body.

The protein created by the Clock gene is particularly common in the eye and a part of the brain known as the suprachiasmatic nucleus, both of which are known to be able to reset the body's biological clock.
